item.title: Identity Services
item.description:
A self-hosted deployment is its own identity provider. Ory Kratos owns user accounts and sign-in, Ory Hydra issues OAuth2 tokens, and the Layer5 Cloud server connects the two to organizations, teams, and roles. Users can sign up with an email address and password, or with Google or GitHub. For how identity fits together as a concept, see Identity and Security.

What the chart configures by default 🔗

Capability Default
Password sign-in On. Minimum 8 characters, checked against known-breached passwords, and rejected when too similar to the account identifier.
Email verification Required before a password sign-in succeeds. Delivered as a code.
Account recovery On, delivered as a code.
Social sign-in Google and GitHub are enabled but have no credentials until you add them.
Login flow lifespan A started sign-in must finish within 12 hours (720m).
Recovery and verification flow lifespan A recovery or verification request stays valid for 30 days (720h).
Registration flow lifespan A started sign-up must finish within 24 hours.
Session lifespan Not set by the chart. Kratos applies its own default. See Sessions.
Access tokens JWT, valid 24 hours. Refresh tokens are valid 1000 hours, ID tokens 1 hour, and authorization codes 1 hour.

Change any of these through the kratos.kratos.config and hydra.hydra.config values. Both are passed to the Ory services unchanged, so the Kratos and Hydra configuration references apply.

item.title: Networking
item.description:
Plan these network paths before you deploy. Most are ordinary HTTPS traffic through your ingress. Real-time co-editing is the exception: it connects browsers directly to each other, and the deployment only introduces them.

Required network paths 🔗

From To Protocol Purpose
Browsers, Meshery Servers, API clients Ingress, public hostname HTTPS UI, API, sign-in (/kratos), and OAuth2 (/hydra)
Browsers Ingress, /collaboration WebSocket over HTTPS Co-editing signaling
Layer5 Cloud server Kratos and Hydra services HTTP, in cluster Account and token operations. Default ports: Kratos public 9010 and admin 9011, Hydra public 4444 and admin 4445
Kratos Layer5 Cloud server HTTP, in cluster Registration hooks, and identity mail when the HTTP courier is selected
Layer5 Cloud server, Kratos, Hydra PostgreSQL TCP 5432 Databases meshery, kratos, hydra
Layer5 Cloud server SMTP relay SMTP on 25, 465, 587, or 2525 Mail. The relay must resolve to a public address
Layer5 Cloud server Webhook receivers HTTPS Optional webhooks
Layer5 Cloud server OpenTelemetry collector OTLP gRPC Optional traces
Browsers Public STUN and TURN hosts UDP and TCP Direct connections between co-editing browsers

The ingress must support WebSocket upgrades. A controller or load balancer that closes idle connections shorter than the signaling keep-alive (below) disconnects users from their co-editing session.

item.title: Monitoring
item.description:
Layer5 Cloud gives you four signals: two health endpoints, structured logs with stable error codes, a set of startup messages that tell you whether the deployment is fully working, and optional OpenTelemetry traces. It does not expose a Prometheus metrics endpoint, so build service-level indicators from ingress and Kubernetes metrics plus the signals below.

Health endpoints 🔗

Endpoint Answers Meaning
GET /healthz 200 with the text Cloud is live The process is running. The chart uses it for the liveness probe.
GET /readyz 200 when ready, 503 before The server finished startup and is serving. The chart uses it for the readiness and startup probes.

Both endpoints are unauthenticated. The startup probe allows 20 failed checks at 10-second intervals, so a slow start gets about 200 seconds before Kubernetes restarts the pod. Database migrations run before the server reports ready, so an upgrade that carries a large migration can approach that limit.
